content.text: Cycle model is a pure passthrough — its 3632 is whatever **vsim itself** prints, with no driver instrumentation. Hybrid reports `vsim_mcycle - qemu_mcycle` across the PC window. The red flag: if 3632 is the *whole program* and 14707 is a *sub-window* of it, a subset cannot exceed the whole — that points to either different regions being compared or overhead leaking into the window delta. Let me pin down three things: what vsim prints in cycle mode, whether resume/drain DMI overhead leaks into mcycle, and the actual demo commands.

<cell id="cell-0"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type># andes-sim demo: how many cycles does `hello` take?

`andes-sim` runs one RISC-V binary on three models with one command:

| Model    | What it is                                      | Speed | Gives you |
|----------|-------------------------------------------------|-------|-----------|
| `fast`   | functional simulation (QEMU)                    | MHz   | program output, instantly |
| `cycle`  | the real Andes core RTL (Verilator)             | kHz   | exact whole-program cycles |
| `hybrid` | `fast` skips ahead, `cycle` measures one region | ~MHz  | exact cycles for the region you mark |

This demo builds one `hello` program and runs it on all three. No engine
knowledge needed: you write C, compile once, and pick a model at run time.</cell id="cell-0">
<cell id="cell-1">import os
from pathlib import Path
root = next(str(d) for d in (Path.cwd(), *Path.cwd().parents)
            if (d / "build" / "andes-sim").exists())
os.chdir(root)
os.environ["PATH"] = f"{root}/build:" + os.environ["PATH"]
print("working dir:", root)</cell id="cell-1">

working dir: /home/nick/work/hybrid_sim

<cell id="cell-2"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type>## 1. Build `hello`

One compile command. The two flags `-B build/runtime -specs=andes-sim.specs`
link the portable runtime, so the same ELF runs on every engine.</cell id="cell-2">
<cell id="cell-3">%%bash
. ./config.env 2>/dev/null      # sets HYBRID_TOOLCHAIN
GCC="$HYBRID_TOOLCHAIN/bin/riscv64-unknown-elf-gcc"

cat > hello.c <<'EOF'
#include <stdio.h>

int main(void)
{
  printf("hello\n");
  return 0;
}
EOF

"$GCC" -march=rv64gc -mabi=lp64d -O1 \
  -B build/runtime -specs=andes-sim.specs hello.c -o hello.elf

echo "built:"; file hello.elf</cell id="cell-3">

<cell id="cell-4"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type>## 2. Run it fast

`--model fast` answers "does my program work?" in well under a second.</cell id="cell-4">
<cell id="cell-5">!andes-sim run --model fast hello.elf</cell id="cell-5">

hello

<cell id="cell-6"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type>## 3. Same binary, cycle accurate

`--model cycle` runs the same ELF on the real Andes core RTL. No rebuild.
The `cycles simulated` line is the exact whole-program cycle count.

(This repo has several RTL engines built, so we name one with `--engine`.)</cell id="cell-6">
<cell id="cell-7">!andes-sim run --model cycle --engine vsim:ax45mpv_premium hello.elf</cell id="cell-7">

[info] hart 0 reset vector: 0x100000
[info] sim_control: received command 0x0
[info] sim_control: got exit 0, stopping
[info] Exit PC: 100480
[info] Core 0 last PCs: 0x100480 0x100482 
[info] 3632 cycles simulated
[info] 0.441s elapsed, 8235.828Hz

Version : unknown

<cell id="cell-8"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type>`hello` finishes in a fraction of a second here, but RTL simulation runs
at kHz: a real workload takes hours this way. And the count includes
everything: boot, runtime setup, exit. Usually you only care about one
region. That is what `hybrid` is for.

## 4. Mark the region you care about

Wrap the region with two markers from `<andes_sim/ROI.h>` and recompile.
The markers are RISC-V HINT instructions, i.e. NOPs: they cost nothing,
and the marked binary still runs everywhere, even on real silicon.

Here we measure exactly one `printf`:</cell id="cell-8">
<cell id="cell-9">%%bash
. ./config.env 2>/dev/null
GCC="$HYBRID_TOOLCHAIN/bin/riscv64-unknown-elf-gcc"

cat > hello.c <<'EOF'
#include <stdio.h>
#include <andes_sim/ROI.h>

int main(void)
{
  andes_sim_ROI_begin();   /* start measuring here */
  printf("hello\n");
  andes_sim_ROI_end();     /* stop measuring here */
  return 0;
}
EOF

"$GCC" -march=rv64gc -mabi=lp64d -O1 \
  -B build/runtime -specs=andes-sim.specs hello.c -o hello.elf

echo "rebuilt with markers"
</cell id="cell-9">

rebuilt with markers

<cell id="cell-10"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type>### Markers are free

The marked binary is still a normal program. On `fast` (or on silicon) the
markers do nothing:</cell id="cell-10">
<cell id="cell-11">!andes-sim run --model fast hello.elf</cell id="cell-11">

hello

<cell id="cell-12"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type>## 5. Hybrid: skip ahead fast, measure exactly

`--model hybrid --trigger marker` runs everything before the first marker
on the fast engine, then hands the live program state to the RTL engine,
which executes the marked region cycle by cycle.</cell id="cell-12">
<cell id="cell-13">!andes-sim run --model hybrid --trigger marker --engine vsim:ax45mpv_premium hello.elf</cell id="cell-13">

[andes-sim] model=hybrid engine=vsim:ax45mpv_premium vlen=512 trigger=marker fixture=hello
[hsim mmap] 128.0 MiB at /dev/shm (free: 251.9 GiB)
Copyright (C) 2013-2026 Andes Technology Corporation. All rights reserved.
Version : unknown

hello
[marker window_cycles] 14602  (vsim mcycle=789332970270530 - qemu mcycle=789332970255928)
PASS: --model hybrid --trigger marker (hello)

<cell id="cell-14"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type>The answer is the `[marker window_cycles]` line: the exact number of
cycles the marked region (one `printf`) takes on the real core. Program
output still appears, and the run finishes at near-`fast` speed because
only the marked region touches the RTL.

## 6. No markers? The `--pc-start` / `--pc-end` trigger

`--trigger pc` measures between two boundary PCs passed on the command
line as raw `0x` addresses: `--pc-start` (window opens) and `--pc-end`
(window closes). Nothing in the binary needs to cooperate, so this mode
is built for automation: an LLM agent or a script disassembles the
binary, picks two addresses, and composes the run command.

Go back to the plain `hello` from step 1, no markers:</cell id="cell-14">
<cell id="cell-15">%%bash
. ./config.env 2>/dev/null
GCC="$HYBRID_TOOLCHAIN/bin/riscv64-unknown-elf-gcc"

cat > hello.c <<'EOF'
#include <stdio.h>

int main(void)
{
  printf("hello\n");
  return 0;
}
EOF

"$GCC" -march=rv64gc -mabi=lp64d -O1 \
  -B build/runtime -specs=andes-sim.specs hello.c -o hello.elf

echo "rebuilt without markers"
</cell id="cell-15">

rebuilt without markers

<cell id="cell-16"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type>Find the window addresses with `objdump`. Here we measure all of
`main`: from its entry to `_exit`, where the program stops:</cell id="cell-16">
<cell id="cell-17">%%bash
. ./config.env 2>/dev/null
"$HYBRID_TOOLCHAIN/bin/riscv64-unknown-elf-objdump" -d hello.elf | grep -E '<(main|_exit)>:'</cell id="cell-17">

0000000000100074 <main>:
0000000000100474 <_exit>:

<cell id="cell-18"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type>Take the two addresses and pass them as the window boundaries:</cell id="cell-18">
<cell id="cell-19">!andes-sim run --model hybrid --trigger pc --pc-start 0x100074 --pc-end 0x100474 --engine vsim:ax45mpv_premium hello.elf</cell id="cell-19">

[andes-sim] model=hybrid engine=vsim:ax45mpv_premium vlen=512 trigger=pc fixture=hello
[hsim mmap] 128.0 MiB at /dev/shm (free: 251.9 GiB)
Copyright (C) 2013-2026 Andes Technology Corporation. All rights reserved.
Version : unknown

hello
[pc window_cycles] 14707  (vsim mcycle=789388570456955 - qemu mcycle=789388570442248)
PASS: --model hybrid --trigger pc (hello)

<cell id="cell-20"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type>Same idea, no markers: `[pc window_cycles]` is the exact cycle count
between the two boundary PCs on the real core. It lands close to the
marker figure above; the small extra is `main`'s prologue and the C
runtime's exit path, which the markers excluded.

## Recap

One source, one compile command, three models, two ways to pick a region:

| Goal                              | Command |
|-----------------------------------|---------|
| Does it work? (instant)           | `andes-sim run --model fast hello.elf` |
| Whole-program cycles (slow)       | `andes-sim run --model cycle --engine vsim:ax45mpv_premium hello.elf` |
| Cycles for the marked region      | `andes-sim run --model hybrid --trigger marker --engine vsim:ax45mpv_premium hello.elf` |
| Same, without touching the source | `andes-sim run --model hybrid --trigger pc --pc-start 0x100074 --pc-end 0x100474 --engine vsim:ax45mpv_premium hello.elf` |

To measure your own program: `#include <andes_sim/ROI.h>`, wrap the region
with `andes_sim_ROI_begin()` / `andes_sim_ROI_end()`, rebuild with the same
two flags, run `hybrid`. If you cannot edit the source, find two boundary
addresses with `objdump` and pass them with `--trigger pc`.

More: `docs/andes_sim_tutorial.ipynb` (all trigger modes and engines),
`docs/USER_GUIDE.md` (full reference).</cell id="cell-20">

content.text: `get_cycles()` is the key: it returns `sc_time_stamp() / clock_period` — **total SystemC simulation clock cycles** from sim start to exit. That is a fundamentally different counter from the hybrid path, which reports the drained **`mcycle` CSR delta**. For a normal run both track real cycles ~1:1, and `mcycle` ≤ sim-cycles, so the whole program's `mcycle` is ≤ 3632. A sub-window reporting 14602 therefore means the hybrid `mcycle` delta is counting something beyond real ROI execution. The prime suspect: Debug-Module resume/drain DMI handshake cycles leaking into `mcycle` while the hart is halted. Let me confirm the drain/resume ordering and run the decisive tiny-window experiment.

name: project_hybrid_cache_csr_not_transported
description: hybrid handoff omits Andes mcache_ctl(0x7CA)/mmisc_ctl(0x7D0), so vsim resumes with caches OFF -> window cycles ~4x inflated vs cycle model
metadata:
  type: project
---

The hybrid handoff ABI (`include/hybrid/state_abi.h` `hybrid_state_v1`) does NOT
carry the Andes custom setup CSRs `mcache_ctl` (0x7CA) or `mmisc_ctl` (0x7D0).
crt0 (`_start`) enables the L1 I/D caches in its first 3 instructions
(`csrsi mcache_ctl,1; csrw mcache_ctl,0x703`). On a `cycle` run or a hybrid
window that starts at `_start`, vsim executes that write -> caches ON. On a
hybrid window whose handoff point is AFTER crt0 (e.g. `--trigger pc --pc-start <main>`
or `--trigger marker`), QEMU runs crt0 (QEMU has no cache model), then vsim
resumes with `mcache_ctl` at reset = caches OFF. The whole measured region then
runs uncached -> ~4x inflated window_cycles.

**Demo evidence** (andes_sim_demo.ipynb, hello.elf, engine vsim:ax45mpv_premium):
- `cycle` whole-program = 3632 cycles (caches on)
- hybrid pc [_start 0x100000, _exit 0x100474] = 3370 (caches on, ~matches cycle)
- hybrid pc [main 0x100074, _exit 0x100474] = 14707 (caches OFF) <- the puzzling 4x
- hybrid pc [main, main+4] 2 insns = 74 (~37 cyc/insn = uncached latency)
A superset window (3370) cheaper than its subset (14707) is impossible unless
cache-enable state differs -> proves the missing CSR.

**Why:** functional engine (QEMU) has no microarch state; the cache-enable bit
lives in a custom CSR that is not part of the transported architectural state.

**How to apply:** when a hybrid window looks inflated vs the cycle model, suspect
caches-off-on-resume first. Proper fix: add mcache_ctl (+mmisc_ctl) to
hybrid_state_v1, drain in `qemu_plugin/hybrid_handoff.c`, restore in
`ResumeDriver::resume()` (verilator/src/hybrid/resume_driver.hpp). Caveat: only
works if QEMU's andes target stores the CSR write; else ResumeDriver must set the
engine's cache-enable value directly. The F16 warmup-interval machinery
(`StateDrain::set_warmup_snapshot`, `mcycle_at_measure_start`) is a partial
mitigation but does not fix caches being disabled outright. Related: [[project_vsim_halt_slack]].

content.text:
No, the 14707 does not make sense as a real region cost. The 3632 is correct; the hybrid figure is ~4x inflated by a handoff bug.

**What each number actually is**
- `cycle` 3632 = whole-program clock cycles (`sc_time/period`, `main.cpp:682`), vsim native RAM, **caches enabled**.
- `hybrid --trigger pc` 14707 = drained `mcycle` delta over `[main, _exit]`, vsim resumed from QEMU, **caches disabled**.

**Why it's impossible as-is.** A region is a subset of the whole program, so on the same core it can't cost more than the whole program. I measured (same engine, same `hello.elf`):

| hybrid pc window | cycles |
|---|---|
| `[_start 0x100000, _exit 0x100474]` ≈ whole program | **3370** |
| `[main 0x100074, _exit 0x100474]` (the demo) | **14707** |
| `[main, main+4]` 2 instructions, no `printf` | **74** |

The superset (3370) is *cheaper* than its subset (14707). The only thing that explains that is different cache state.

**Root cause.** crt0 turns the L1 caches on in its first 3 instructions:
```
100000: csrsi mcache_ctl,1       # mcache_ctl = Andes CSR 0x7CA
100008: csrw  mcache_ctl,0x703   # I-cache + D-cache + prefetch ON
```
- `cycle` model and `[_start,...]` run this write **on vsim** → caches on → 3632 / 3370.
- `[main,...]` and `marker`: QEMU runs crt0 (QEMU has no cache model), then vsim resumes at `main`. `mcache_ctl` (0x7CA) is **not in the handoff ABI** (`state_abi.h` carries only mstatus/mepc/.../pmp/V) and **not restored by `ResumeDriver`**, so vsim resumes with `mcache_ctl` at reset = **caches off**. The whole `printf` path runs uncached. (74 cyc / 2 instructions ≈ 37 cyc each = uncached latency — consistent.)

So `mcache_ctl` (and `mmisc_ctl` 0x7D0, set at `0x100032`) are silently dropped at the boundary.

**Fix.** Add `mcache_ctl` (+`mmisc_ctl`) to `hybrid_state_v1`, drain in `qemu_plugin/hybrid_handoff.c`, restore in `ResumeDriver::resume()`. `[main,_exit]` should then fall to ~3000. Caveat: works only if QEMU's andes target *stores* the CSR write; if QEMU ignores it, `ResumeDriver` must set the engine's cache-enable value directly.

Want me to implement + verify the fix (TDD: failing test that `[main,_exit]` ≈ cycle-model cost, then transport the CSR)?

The `verilator/tests/hybrid/*.test.cpp` doctest unit tests are header-only
(C++20 + ABI header) and run directly on the host - no podman/Verilator needed.
Build+run one with:

```sh
cd /home/nick/work/hybrid_sim
g++ -std=c++20 -I verilator/src -I verilator/tests/hybrid -I include \
    -I verilator/external/doctest/doctest \
    verilator/tests/hybrid/resume_driver.test.cpp -o /tmp/t && /tmp/t
```

`-I verilator/tests/hybrid` is only needed for tests that include the shared
`recording_bus.hpp` (e.g. state_drain). This is the fast RED/GREEN loop; the
canonical container/ctest path is only required for the e2e suite.

Exceptions that do NOT link on the host: `qemu_handback.test.cpp` (needs libfmt:
`undefined reference to fmt::v11::...`), and the SystemC-dependent ones
(`*_smoke.cpp`, `shared_mem_offset.test.cpp`). Skip those on host.

vsim rebuild after editing `src/hybrid/*.hpp` or `src/simulator.hpp`:
`bash scripts/build_vsim.sh` (podman; incremental, recompiles `main.cpp.o` only,
RTL is cached - ~30s). Then e2e: `JOBS=8 FILTER=rt_c_v bash scripts/run_e2e.sh`.

  (`engine_registry.cpp:46,54`). The V-register scratch address is NO LONGER a
  fixed constant -- it is the mmap's top page (`v_scratch_gpa(ram_base,
  ram_size)`, L26), derived from the runtime RAM base + size, so it adapts to
  any base and is no longer a porting blocker. The retired Python golden
  (`tools/orchestrator/spawn.py`) keeps its own hardcoded copies.
- Where: `driver/engine_registry.cpp:46,54`.
- Status: PARTIALLY RELAXED: engine variant + VLEN are pluggable, and the
  scratch GPA is now runtime-derived (L26); the machine and the CPU family are
  still literals that block porting to another core.

### L11. [RESOLVED 2026-06-12: ceiling raised to VLEN 1024, over-limit aborts] VLEN ceiling  (F-T3.4)

- Was: the wire format reserved 64 bytes per vector register (VLEN 512)
  and the plugin CLAMPED the drained bytes to that with no warning - a
  wider engine silently lost the upper bytes of every V register. The
  standalone fast model also hardcoded `vlen=512`.
- Now (supported range: VLEN 128..1024):

name: project_hybrid_cache_csr_not_transported
description: FIXED - hybrid handoff now transports Andes mcache_ctl(0x7CA)/mmisc_ctl(0x7D0); was causing ~4x inflated post-crt0 window cycles (caches resumed OFF)
metadata:
  type: project
---

FIXED (2026-06-16, branch code-review). The hybrid handoff ABI did NOT carry the
Andes custom setup CSRs `mcache_ctl` (0x7CA) or `mmisc_ctl` (0x7D0). crt0
(`_start`) enables the L1 I/D caches in its first 3 instructions
(`csrsi mcache_ctl,1; csrw mcache_ctl,0x703`). A hybrid window whose handoff
point is AFTER crt0 (`--trigger pc --pc-start <main>`, or `--trigger marker`)
ran QEMU through crt0 (QEMU has no cache model), then vsim resumed with
`mcache_ctl` at reset = caches OFF -> whole measured region ran uncached -> ~4x
inflated window_cycles vs the cycle model.

**Symptom to recognize:** a hybrid window reports MORE cycles than the
whole-program cycle model, or a smaller sub-window costs more than a superset
that starts at `_start`. That superset-cheaper-than-subset is impossible unless
cache-enable state differs -> suspect a dropped machine-setup CSR.

**The fix (4 edit sites, the standard transport pattern):**
- `include/hybrid/state_abi.h`: added `uint64_t mcache_ctl; uint64_t mmisc_ctl;`
  after `fcsr`, shrank `reserved[208]->[192]` (size unchanged, no version bump);
  updated `state_abi_check.h` offset asserts.
- `qemu_plugin/hybrid_handoff.c`: VcpuRegs handles + `find_reg("mcache_ctl"/"mmisc_ctl")`
  + `s.mcache_ctl/mmisc_ctl = read_reg64(...)` in drain_state_into.
- `verilator/src/hybrid/resume_driver.hpp`: `kCsrMcacheCtl=0x7CA`, `kCsrMmiscCtl=0x7D0`;
  `write_csr_tolerant(...)` for both, placed BEFORE the mcycle restore.
- Tests: new resume unit case + ABI layout asserts (host doctest), all 43 e2e pass.

**Why QEMU transport works:** QEMU's Andes fork stores these (write_mcache_ctl
masks+stores into env->andes_csr), `andes_csr_init` merges andes_csr_ops into the
global csr_ops, and the gdbstub csr feature emits them by name (predicate
isz_dsz passes when caches are configured). The plugin reads them by name.

**Verified:** hybrid pc `[main 0x100074, _exit 0x100474]` on hello.elf dropped
14707 -> 2871 cycles (now < whole-program 3632, the correct subset relationship).

mdcm_cfg, mxstatus, ...) are still not transported; only the cache/misc-ctl pair
is. Docs: CLAUDE.md "CSR restore split" updated; limitations notebook L21 ->

description: FIXED - hybrid handoff now transports Andes mcache_ctl(0x7CA)/mmisc_ctl(0x7D0); was causing ~4x inflated post-crt0 window cycles (caches resumed OFF)
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: project
  originSessionId: deb9f9b8-9454-4a56-b6d0-4520be19606f
---

FIXED (2026-06-16, branch code-review). The hybrid handoff ABI did NOT carry the
Andes custom setup CSRs `mcache_ctl` (0x7CA) or `mmisc_ctl` (0x7D0). crt0
(`_start`) enables the L1 I/D caches in its first 3 instructions
(`csrsi mcache_ctl,1; csrw mcache_ctl,0x703`). A hybrid window whose handoff
point is AFTER crt0 (`--trigger pc --pc-start <main>`, or `--trigger marker`)
ran QEMU through crt0 (QEMU has no cache model), then vsim resumed with
`mcache_ctl` at reset = caches OFF -> whole measured region ran uncached -> ~4x
inflated window_cycles vs the cycle model.

**Symptom to recognize:** a hybrid window reports MORE cycles than the
whole-program cycle model, or a smaller sub-window costs more than a superset
that starts at `_start`. That superset-cheaper-than-subset is impossible unless
cache-enable state differs -> suspect a dropped machine-setup CSR.

**The fix (4 edit sites, the standard transport pattern):**
- `include/hybrid/state_abi.h`: added `uint64_t mcache_ctl; uint64_t mmisc_ctl;`
  after `fcsr`, shrank `reserved[208]->[192]` (size unchanged, no version bump);
  updated `state_abi_check.h` offset asserts.
- `qemu_plugin/hybrid_handoff.c`: VcpuRegs handles + `find_reg("mcache_ctl"/"mmisc_ctl")`
  + `s.mcache_ctl/mmisc_ctl = read_reg64(...)` in drain_state_into.
- `verilator/src/hybrid/resume_driver.hpp`: `kCsrMcacheCtl=0x7CA`, `kCsrMmiscCtl=0x7D0`;
  `write_csr_tolerant(...)` for both, placed BEFORE the mcycle restore.
- Tests: new resume unit case + ABI layout asserts (host doctest), all 43 e2e pass.

**Why QEMU transport works:** QEMU's Andes fork stores these (write_mcache_ctl
masks+stores into env->andes_csr), `andes_csr_init` merges andes_csr_ops into the
global csr_ops, and the gdbstub csr feature emits them by name (predicate
isz_dsz passes when caches are configured). The plugin reads them by name.

**Verified:** hybrid pc `[main 0x100074, _exit 0x100474]` on hello.elf dropped
14707 -> 2871 cycles (now < whole-program 3632, the correct subset relationship).

**Still open (rest of L21):** other Andes vendor CSRs (mmsc_cfg, micm_cfg,
mdcm_cfg, mxstatus, ...) are still not transported; only the cache/misc-ctl pair
is. Docs: CLAUDE.md "CSR restore split" updated; limitations notebook L21 ->
PARTIAL (quick-ref + Tier-3 cell + demo notebook re-run still pending). Related:
[[project_vsim_halt_slack]].

---
name: project_hybrid_cache_csr_not_transported
description: "hybrid handoff omits Andes mcache_ctl(0x7CA)/mmisc_ctl(0x7D0), so vsim resumes with caches OFF -> window cycles ~4x inflated vs cycle model"
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: project
  originSessionId: deb9f9b8-9454-4a56-b6d0-4520be19606f
---

The hybrid handoff ABI (`include/hybrid/state_abi.h` `hybrid_state_v1`) does NOT
carry the Andes custom setup CSRs `mcache_ctl` (0x7CA) or `mmisc_ctl` (0x7D0).
crt0 (`_start`) enables the L1 I/D caches in its first 3 instructions
(`csrsi mcache_ctl,1; csrw mcache_ctl,0x703`). On a `cycle` run or a hybrid
window that starts at `_start`, vsim executes that write -> caches ON. On a
hybrid window whose handoff point is AFTER crt0 (e.g. `--trigger pc --pc-start <main>`
or `--trigger marker`), QEMU runs crt0 (QEMU has no cache model), then vsim
resumes with `mcache_ctl` at reset = caches OFF. The whole measured region then
runs uncached -> ~4x inflated window_cycles.

**Demo evidence** (andes_sim_demo.ipynb, hello.elf, engine vsim:ax45mpv_premium):
- `cycle` whole-program = 3632 cycles (caches on)
- hybrid pc [_start 0x100000, _exit 0x100474] = 3370 (caches on, ~matches cycle)
- hybrid pc [main 0x100074, _exit 0x100474] = 14707 (caches OFF) <- the puzzling 4x
- hybrid pc [main, main+4] 2 insns = 74 (~37 cyc/insn = uncached latency)
A superset window (3370) cheaper than its subset (14707) is impossible unless
cache-enable state differs -> proves the missing CSR.

**Why:** functional engine (QEMU) has no microarch state; the cache-enable bit
lives in a custom CSR that is not part of the transported architectural state.

**How to apply:** when a hybrid window looks inflated vs the cycle model, suspect
caches-off-on-resume first. Proper fix: add mcache_ctl (+mmisc_ctl) to
hybrid_state_v1, drain in `qemu_plugin/hybrid_handoff.c`, restore in
`ResumeDriver::resume()` (verilator/src/hybrid/resume_driver.hpp). Caveat: only
works if QEMU's andes target stores the CSR write; else ResumeDriver must set the
engine's cache-enable value directly. The F16 warmup-interval machinery
(`StateDrain::set_warmup_snapshot`, `mcycle_at_measure_start`) is a partial
mitigation but does not fix caches being disabled outright. Related: [[project_vsim_halt_slack]].

Done. The fix is implemented, tested, and verified end-to-end.

## Result
`hybrid pc [main, _exit]` on `hello.elf`: **14707 → 2871 cycles**. Now *below* the whole-program `cycle` figure (3632), which is the physically correct subset relationship. Root cause was exactly as diagnosed: crt0's `csrw mcache_ctl,0x703` (L1 cache enable) ran on the cache-less functional engine and wasn't carried across the handoff, so vsim resumed with caches off.

## What changed (transport the two Andes setup CSRs)
| Site | Edit |
|---|---|
| `include/hybrid/state_abi.h` (+asserts) | added `mcache_ctl` + `mmisc_ctl`, `reserved[208→192]` (size unchanged, no version bump) |
| `qemu_plugin/hybrid_handoff.c` | drain both via gdbstub by name |
| `verilator/src/hybrid/resume_driver.hpp` | `kCsrMcacheCtl=0x7CA`/`kCsrMmiscCtl=0x7D0`, tolerant restore before the `mcycle` restore |
| CLAUDE.md | CSR-restore-split paragraph updated |

## TDD trail
- **Structural first:** ABI fields + layout asserts → existing tests stay green (behavior-neutral).
- **RED:** new `resume_driver` unit test asserting the DMI write to 0x7CA/0x7D0 — failed (no such write).
- **GREEN:** added the tolerant restore — test passes.
- **Regression:** 18/18 host unit suites, **43/43 e2e** (21 marker + 21 pc + 1 neg, all `--verify`), so the cache-enable restore round-trips correctly across asm/C/V/S-U fixtures.

Tolerant writes mean a non-Andes engine just no-ops the CSR; a drained 0 restores the reset state. QEMU cooperated (it stores the CSR and exposes it via gdbstub), which the cycle drop confirms.

## Two doc artifacts still stale (recommend I fix next)
1. **`docs/andes_sim_demo.ipynb`** — the notebook you were looking at still shows 14707 with the cell-20 explanation ("small extra is prologue + exit path"), which actually described the bug. It needs a re-run (new outputs) + a short narrative fix. This closes the loop on your original question.
2. **`docs/andes_sim_limitations.ipynb` L21** — "Andes vendor CSRs not transported" should move `open → partial` (cache pair done; `mmsc_cfg`/`micm_cfg`/`mxstatus`/... still open). 5 cells reference it.

## State coverage: what the wire format carries

Inventory view of the ROI rule above. Everything below is checked against
`include/hybrid/state_abi.h` (struct), the QEMU plugin drain
(`qemu_plugin/hybrid_handoff.c`), the vsim resume (`resume_driver.hpp`),
and the vsim drain (`state_drain.hpp`).

### Carried in `hybrid_state_v1`

- 32 GPRs, 32 FPRs
- `fcsr` (frm + sticky fflags; added 2026-06-12, closing L20)
- 13 M-mode CSRs: `mstatus, mepc, mtvec, mcause, mtval, mscratch,
  medeleg, mideleg, mip, mie, mcycle, minstret, satp`
- PMP: 16 `pmpcfg` + 64 `pmpaddr`
- V extension: `vstart, vtype, vl, vlenb, vreg[32], vxsat, vxrm, vcsr`
- F13 warmup metadata: `mcycle_at_measure_start`, `minstret_at_measure_start`
- `reserved[208]` = room for ~26 more `uint64` (wire format is version 2
  since L11 widened `vreg[]` to 128 bytes per register)

### NOT in the wire format at all

- All S-mode CSRs: `stvec, sepc, scause, stval, sscratch, sie, sip,
  scounteren, senvcfg, stimecmp`
- HPM block: `mhpmcounter3..31`, `mhpmevent3..31`, `mcounteren,
  menvcfg, mcountinhibit, mconfigptr, misa, time`
- Every Andes-custom CSR (`mmsc_cfg, mcache_ctl, mmisc_ctl, micm_cfg,
  mdcm_cfg, mxstatus, mdcause, mnvec`, ...). See L21.

### Carried but NOT restored into vsim

The QEMU1 plugin drains them into the struct, but `ResumeDriver`
writes none of them into the vsim hart. They are dead during the ROI:

- `satp` (L3) and `medeleg, mideleg` (L4) -- S-mode CSRs the M-only
  default engine does not implement. (`mscratch` left this set in L23;
  `mepc / mcause / mtval / mie / mip` left it in L24 -- all writable
  M-mode CSRs that round-trip now.) PMP is restored only for
  S/U-privilege handoffs (L6, 2026-06-13) -- without it an S/U ROI
  cannot fetch on a PMP-implementing core; M-mode handoffs keep PMP
  pass-through-only.

CSRs actually restored into vsim: `mstatus, mtvec, mscratch (L23),
mepc, mcause, mtval, mie, mip (L24), mcycle, minstret, fcsr`, plus
`dcsr.prv` (the privilege level, verified after write) and the PMP block
for S/U handoffs (`resume_driver.hpp`). The writable M-mode CSRs are
re-read at drain and compared by `--verify`, except `mip` (restored +
re-read but not compared -- its pending bits are hardware-driven and
diverge between the engines' clocks).

### Transport ceiling - why "all CSRs" is not free

Three surfaces, three ceilings:

| Surface         | Mechanism                                     | Ceiling |
|-----------------|-----------------------------------------------|---------|
| QEMU1 drain     | plugin reads by NAME from gdbstub XML         | only CSRs the QEMU fork advertises |
| vsim resume     | DMI Abstract Cmd + Program Buffer (by number) | RO / WARL / locked bits will not take arbitrary values |
| vsim drain      | DMI Abstract read (by number)                 | general for any readable CSR |

Two structural blockers to "all CSRs":

1. Wire format is a fixed C struct; `reserved[208]` fits about 26 more
   `uint64`. Reaching the full M + S + HPM + Andes set needs a v2 layout.
2. Semantics, not just bits. Restore order and side effects already bite
   (`mstatus.FS/VS` gating, `vsetvl` atomicity for `vtype/vl`). Writing
   `satp` flushes the TLB; Andes `mcache_ctl / mmisc_ctl` toggle caches,
   prefetchers, branch prediction and may be RO or locked when written
   via the debug module mid-run. Those are exactly the CSRs that shape
   the cycle figure.

Verdict: extending the wire format to a bounded set in this way is
feasible - the L20 fix is the worked example (one `uint64` carved from
`reserved[]`, drained by name, restored via the existing
abstract-or-PB write, read back at drain). S-mode trap CSRs and a
chosen Andes microarch subset can follow the same recipe.
"All RISC-V CSRs including Andes-specific" is not feasible without
redesigning the wire format and lifting the entire ROI envelope (L2-L6).

content.text:
`/simplify → 4 cleanup agents in parallel → apply the fixes`

You are improving the quality of the changed code, not hunting for bugs. Review
it for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude issues, then fix what you
find. Do not look for correctness bugs — that is what `/code-review` is for.

## Phase 0 — Gather the diff

Run `git diff @{upstream}...HEAD` (or `git diff main...HEAD` / `git diff HEAD~1`
if there's no upstream) to get the unified diff under review. If there are
uncommitted changes, or the range diff is empty, also run `git diff HEAD` and
include the working-tree changes in scope — the review often runs before the
commit. If a PR number, branch name, or file path was passed as an argument,
review that target instead. Treat this diff as the review scope.

## Phase 1 — Review (4 cleanup agents in parallel)

Launch **4 independent review agents** via the Agent tool, all in a
single message so they run concurrently. Pass each agent the diff and one of
the four angles below. Each returns its findings with `file`, `line`, a
one-line `summary`, and the concrete cost (what is duplicated, wasted, or
harder to maintain).

### Reuse

Flag new code that re-implements something the codebase
already has — Grep shared/utility modules and files adjacent to the change,
and name the existing helper to call instead.

### Simplification

Flag unnecessary complexity the diff adds: redundant or derivable state,
copy-paste with slight variation, deep nesting, dead code left behind. Name
the simpler form that does the same job.

### Efficiency

Flag wasted work the diff introduces: redundant computation or repeated I/O,
independent operations run sequentially, blocking work added to startup or
hot paths. Also flag long-lived objects built from closures or captured
environments — they keep the entire enclosing scope alive for the object's
lifetime (a memory leak when that scope holds large values); prefer a
class/struct that copies only the fields it needs. Name the cheaper
alternative.

### Altitude

Check that each change is implemented at the right depth, not as a fragile
bandaid. Special cases layered on shared infrastructure are a sign the fix
isn't deep enough — prefer generalizing the underlying mechanism over adding
special cases.

## Phase 2 — Apply the fixes

Wait for all four agents to complete, dedup findings that point at the same
line or mechanism, and fix each remaining one directly. Skip any finding whose
fix would change intended behavior, require changes well outside the reviewed
diff, or that you judge to be a false positive — note the skip rather than
arguing with it. Finish with a brief summary of what was fixed and what was
skipped (or confirm the code was already clean).

content.text:
## The puzzle

You saw two numbers for the same `hello` program on the same core:
- `cycle` model (whole program): **3632 cycles**
- `hybrid` (just the `main` region): **14707 cycles**

This is impossible on its face. The `main` region is a *part* of the whole program. A part cannot cost more than the whole. So something was wrong.

## Root cause: the cache switch was lost at the handoff

**1. Caches make the CPU fast.** A cache is small fast memory next to the CPU. When caches are ON, the program runs fast. When caches are OFF, every instruction fetch and every memory read goes all the way to main memory, which is slow - roughly 5x slower here.

**2. Caches start OFF. Startup code turns them ON.** When the chip resets, caches are disabled. The very first startup code (`crt0`, which runs before `main`) flips them on. You can see it in the first 3 instructions:
```
csrw mcache_ctl, 0x703   # mcache_ctl = a control register (a switch); 0x703 = "I-cache + D-cache ON"
```
`mcache_ctl` is an Andes-specific control register (CSR number `0x7CA`). Think of it as the cache on/off switch.

**3. The two engines are different.**
- **QEMU** (the fast functional engine) does **not** simulate caches at all. It just runs instructions and gets the right answer. It stores the value `0x703` in its copy of `mcache_ctl`, but that value means nothing to QEMU - it has no caches to turn on.
- **vsim** (the cycle-accurate engine) *does* simulate caches, and they obey `mcache_ctl`.

**4. The handoff dropped the switch.** In `hybrid` mode with a `pc` or `marker` trigger:
- QEMU runs the startup (`crt0`), so the cache switch gets set to ON - but only inside QEMU, where it does nothing.
- Then QEMU hands the program state to vsim and vsim takes over at `main`.
- The handoff copies many registers (GPRs, FPRs, `mstatus`, etc.), **but it never copied `mcache_ctl`**. It was not part of the data format that the two engines exchange.
- So vsim resumed with its cache switch still at the reset default: **OFF**.
- The whole `printf` region then ran with caches off → uncached → ~5x slower → 14707 cycles.

**Why the `cycle` model was correct (3632):** the full `cycle` run executes `crt0` *on vsim itself*. So vsim flipped its own cache switch ON before reaching `main`. Only `hybrid` skips `crt0` on vsim (QEMU does it instead), which is exactly why only `hybrid` lost the switch.

The clean proof: a hybrid window starting at `_start` (so vsim runs `crt0`) gave **3370** - matching the cycle model. A window starting at `main` (vsim skips `crt0`) gave **14707**. Same code, only difference is whether vsim ran the cache-enable instruction.

## The solution: carry the cache switch across the handoff

The handoff already copies CPU state from QEMU to vsim through a shared data structure (`hybrid_state_v1`). The fix is to add the cache switch to that copy, the same way every other register is handled. Three steps, mirroring how `fcsr`/`mscratch` are already transported:

1. **Add a slot for it** in the shared format (`state_abi.h`): two new fields, `mcache_ctl` and `mmisc_ctl` (a sibling config register `crt0` also sets).
2. **QEMU writes the switch value into that slot** (`hybrid_handoff.c`): read `mcache_ctl` from QEMU by name and store `0x703` in the handoff data.
3. **vsim reads the slot and sets its own switch** (`resume_driver.hpp`): on resume, write `mcache_ctl` into the vsim hart, so its caches turn ON before the measured region runs.

The write is "tolerant": if some other engine does not have this Andes register, the write is harmlessly ignored.

**Result:** the `main` window dropped from **14707 → 2871** cycles - now below the whole-program 3632, which is the correct relationship (a part costs less than the whole).

One honest limitation: vsim's caches now turn on, but they start *empty* (cold). The first accesses still pay a one-time warm-up cost. That is normal and expected for any hybrid simulator, and the existing `--vsim-warmup-icount` option exists to exclude that warm-up if you only want steady-state numbers. The bug was not cold caches - it was caches being switched **off entirely**.

FIXED (2026-06-16, branch code-review). The hybrid handoff ABI did NOT carry the
Andes custom setup CSRs `mcache_ctl` (0x7CA) or `mmisc_ctl` (0x7D0). crt0
(`_start`) enables the L1 I/D caches in its first 3 instructions
(`csrsi mcache_ctl,1; csrw mcache_ctl,0x703`). A hybrid window whose handoff
point is AFTER crt0 (`--trigger pc --pc-start <main>`, or `--trigger marker`)
ran QEMU through crt0 (QEMU has no cache model), then vsim resumed with
`mcache_ctl` at reset = caches OFF -> whole measured region ran uncached -> ~4x
inflated window_cycles vs the cycle model.

**Symptom to recognize:** a hybrid window reports MORE cycles than the
whole-program cycle model, or a smaller sub-window costs more than a superset
that starts at `_start`. That superset-cheaper-than-subset is impossible unless
cache-enable state differs -> suspect a dropped machine-setup CSR.

**The fix (4 edit sites, the standard transport pattern):**
- `include/hybrid/state_abi.h`: added `uint64_t mcache_ctl; uint64_t mmisc_ctl;`
  after `fcsr`, shrank `reserved[208]->[192]` (size unchanged, no version bump);
  updated `state_abi_check.h` offset asserts.
- `qemu_plugin/hybrid_handoff.c`: VcpuRegs handles + `find_reg("mcache_ctl"/"mmisc_ctl")`
  + `s.mcache_ctl/mmisc_ctl = read_reg64(...)` in drain_state_into.
- `verilator/src/hybrid/resume_driver.hpp`: `kCsrMcacheCtl=0x7CA`, `kCsrMmiscCtl=0x7D0`;
  `write_csr_tolerant(...)` for both, placed BEFORE the mcycle restore.
- Tests: new resume unit case + ABI layout asserts (host doctest), all 43 e2e pass.

**Why QEMU transport works:** QEMU's Andes fork stores these (write_mcache_ctl
masks+stores into env->andes_csr), `andes_csr_init` merges andes_csr_ops into the
global csr_ops, and the gdbstub csr feature emits them by name (predicate
isz_dsz passes when caches are configured). The plugin reads them by name.

**Verified:** hybrid pc `[main 0x100074, _exit 0x100474]` on hello.elf dropped
14707 -> 2871 cycles (now < whole-program 3632, the correct subset relationship).

**Still open (rest of L21):** other Andes vendor CSRs (mmsc_cfg, micm_cfg,
mdcm_cfg, mxstatus, ...) are still not transported; only the cache/misc-ctl pair
is. Docs: CLAUDE.md "CSR restore split" updated; limitations notebook L21 ->

skills.content:
`/simplify → 4 cleanup agents in parallel → apply the fixes`

You are improving the quality of the changed code, not hunting for bugs. Review
it for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude issues, then fix what you
find. Do not look for correctness bugs — that is what `/code-review` is for.

## Phase 0 — Gather the diff

Run `git diff @{upstream}...HEAD` (or `git diff main...HEAD` / `git diff HEAD~1`
if there's no upstream) to get the unified diff under review. If there are
uncommitted changes, or the range diff is empty, also run `git diff HEAD` and
include the working-tree changes in scope — the review often runs before the
commit. If a PR number, branch name, or file path was passed as an argument,
review that target instead. Treat this diff as the review scope.

## Phase 1 — Review (4 cleanup agents in parallel)

Launch **4 independent review agents** via the Agent tool, all in a
single message so they run concurrently. Pass each agent the diff and one of
the four angles below. Each returns its findings with `file`, `line`, a
one-line `summary`, and the concrete cost (what is duplicated, wasted, or
harder to maintain).

### Reuse

Flag new code that re-implements something the codebase
already has — Grep shared/utility modules and files adjacent to the change,
and name the existing helper to call instead.

### Simplification

Flag unnecessary complexity the diff adds: redundant or derivable state,
copy-paste with slight variation, deep nesting, dead code left behind. Name
the simpler form that does the same job.

### Efficiency

Flag wasted work the diff introduces: redundant computation or repeated I/O,
independent operations run sequentially, blocking work added to startup or
hot paths. Also flag long-lived objects built from closures or captured
environments — they keep the entire enclosing scope alive for the object's
lifetime (a memory leak when that scope holds large values); prefer a
class/struct that copies only the fields it needs. Name the cheaper
alternative.

### Altitude

Check that each change is implemented at the right depth, not as a fragile
bandaid. Special cases layered on shared infrastructure are a sign the fix
isn't deep enough — prefer generalizing the underlying mechanism over adding
special cases.

## Phase 2 — Apply the fixes

Wait for all four agents to complete, dedup findings that point at the same
line or mechanism, and fix each remaining one directly. Skip any finding whose
fix would change intended behavior, require changes well outside the reviewed
diff, or that you judge to be a false positive — note the skip rather than
arguing with it. Finish with a brief summary of what was fixed and what was
skipped (or confirm the code was already clean).

<cell id="cell-0"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type># andes-sim tutorial: measure an RVV GEMM kernel

This tutorial takes one real vector workload - an 8x8x8 integer GEMM
written with RISC-V RVV intrinsics - and answers the question every
kernel writer has: **how many cycles does my kernel take on the real
core?**

You will:

1. build the GEMM and verify it against a plain-C reference,
2. pick a hardware engine and read its RVV parameters (VLEN, DLEN, ...),
3. measure exactly the kernel with ROI markers (`--trigger marker`),
4. find the hot loop with QEMU's hotloop detector and measure it with
   no source edits (`--trigger pc`) - the workflow built for scripts
   and LLM agents.</cell id="cell-0">

<cell id="cell-2"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type>## 1. The program

Three parts, all in one file:

- `init_matrices` - plain C, fills A and B,
- `gemm_rvv` - the kernel, RVV intrinsics. One row of 8 int32 values
  fits in one vector register, so each row of C is computed as
  `C[i][:] += A[i][k] * B[k][:]` with `vle32` / `vmacc` / `vse32`,
- `gemm_c` + a compare loop - the same GEMM in plain C, used to verify
  the vector kernel. The program prints PASS or FAIL itself.

The kernel call is wrapped with the two ROI markers from
`<andes_sim/ROI.h>`. The markers are free (HINT NOPs), so the binary
still runs everywhere. We also add `-g`: debug info lives outside the
loadable image, so it changes nothing in the run - but it lets the
tools show source lines later.</cell id="cell-2">
<cell id="cell-3">%%bash
. ./config.env 2>/dev/null      # sets HYBRID_TOOLCHAIN
GCC="$HYBRID_TOOLCHAIN/bin/riscv64-unknown-elf-gcc"

cat > gemm.c <<'EOF'
/* 8x8x8 integer GEMM: C = A * B.
 * The kernel is RISC-V RVV intrinsics; a plain-C version verifies it. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdint.h>
#include <riscv_vector.h>
#include <andes_sim/ROI.h>

#define N 8

static int32_t A[N][N], B[N][N], C[N][N], C_ref[N][N];

/* init: fill A and B with small signed values (plain C). */
static void init_matrices(void)
{
  for (int i = 0; i < N; i++)
    for (int j = 0; j < N; j++) {
      A[i][j] = (i + j) % 7 - 3;
      B[i][j] = (i * 3 + j) % 5 - 2;
    }
}

/* RVV kernel: row accumulation, C[i][:] += A[i][k] * B[k][:].
 * One row of 8 int32 lanes fits in one vector register (vl = 8).
 * noinline keeps the whole kernel inside the ROI marker span and gives
 * the PC-trigger mode a symbol to anchor on. */
static void __attribute__((noinline)) gemm_rvv(void)
{
  size_t vl = __riscv_vsetvl_e32m1(N);
  for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) {
    vint32m1_t acc = __riscv_vmv_v_x_i32m1(0, vl);
    for (int k = 0; k < N; k++) {
      vint32m1_t brow = __riscv_vle32_v_i32m1(B[k], vl);
      acc = __riscv_vmacc_vx_i32m1(acc, A[i][k], brow, vl);
    }
    __riscv_vse32_v_i32m1(C[i], acc, vl);
  }
}

/* reference: the same GEMM in plain C. */
static void gemm_c(void)
{
  for (int i = 0; i < N; i++)
    for (int j = 0; j < N; j++) {
      int32_t s = 0;
      for (int k = 0; k < N; k++) s += A[i][k] * B[k][j];
      C_ref[i][j] = s;
    }
}

int main(void)
{
  init_matrices();

  andes_sim_ROI_begin();   /* measure the RVV kernel only */
  gemm_rvv();
  andes_sim_ROI_end();

  gemm_c();
  int errors = 0;
  for (int i = 0; i < N; i++)
    for (int j = 0; j < N; j++)
      if (C[i][j] != C_ref[i][j]) errors++;
  if (errors) printf("FAIL: %d mismatches\n", errors);
  else printf("PASS: 8x8x8 RVV GEMM matches the C reference\n");
  return errors != 0;
}
EOF

"$GCC" -march=rv64gcv -mabi=lp64d -O1 -g \
  -B build/runtime -specs=andes-sim.specs gemm.c -o gemm.elf

<cell id="cell-12"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type>QEMU ships a **hotloop detector**: it runs the binary fast and
reports the hottest loops as a Markdown fact sheet made for LLM
consumption. The TL;DR names the hottest loop, its function and source
line - and hands you a ready measure window. We pass the engine's VLEN
to its `--cpu` so the functional run models the same vector hardware:</cell id="cell-12">

QEMU/scripts/hotloops.sh \
  --qemu build/qemu/qemu-system-riscv64 \
  --plugin build/qemu/contrib/plugins/libhotloops.so \
  --cpu "andes-ax45mpv,vext_spec=v1.0,vlen=512" \
  --min-iters 10 gemm.elf</cell id="cell-13">

<cell id="cell-14"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type>## 6. Measure between two PCs

The report computed two ready windows for the hot loop:

- `measure:` - the enclosing function, entry to `ret`. Covers every
  iteration: this is the kernel figure.
- `measure_loop:` - the loop alone, header to the branch fall-through.
  It drains the first time the loop exits, so it covers the FIRST
  complete pass only (here: one row of C, 8 of the 64 iterations).

(The raw `pc_range` is not a window: both pc boundaries fire on their
first hit, so header-to-branch would span a single iteration.)

`--trigger pc` needs nothing from the binary - this is the mode built
for automation: a script or an LLM agent lifts the flags straight from
the report. The whole kernel first:</cell id="cell-14">

## Recap

| Goal                              | Command |
|-----------------------------------|---------|
| Verify the kernel (instant)       | `andes-sim run --model fast gemm.elf` |
| Engine hardware params            | `andes-sim list engines` |
| Kernel cycles via markers         | `andes-sim run --model hybrid --trigger marker --engine vsim:ax45mpv_premium gemm.elf` |
| Hot-loop report (no markers)      | `QEMU/scripts/hotloops.sh --qemu ... --plugin ... gemm.elf` |
| Kernel cycles via boundary PCs    | `andes-sim run --model hybrid --trigger pc --pc-start 0x100078 --pc-end 0x1000c4 --engine vsim:ax45mpv_premium gemm.elf` |
| One pass of the hot loop          | same, with the report's `measure_loop:` flags |

For your own kernel: wrap it with `andes_sim_ROI_begin()` /
`andes_sim_ROI_end()` from `<andes_sim/ROI.h>` and rebuild with the
same two flags - or skip the rebuild entirely: the hotloop detector's
`measure:` line plus `--trigger pc` finds and measures the hot region
with no source edits.

More: `docs/andes_sim_demo.ipynb` (5-minute model tour),
`docs/andes_sim_tutorial.ipynb` (all trigger modes and engines),
`docs/USER_GUIDE.md` (full reference).</cell id="cell-18">

name: project_hybrid_cache_csr_not_transported
description: FIXED - hybrid handoff now transports Andes mcache_ctl(0x7CA)/mmisc_ctl(0x7D0); was causing ~4x inflated post-crt0 window cycles (caches resumed OFF)
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: project
  originSessionId: deb9f9b8-9454-4a56-b6d0-4520be19606f
---

FIXED (2026-06-16, branch code-review). The hybrid handoff ABI did NOT carry the
Andes custom setup CSRs `mcache_ctl` (0x7CA) or `mmisc_ctl` (0x7D0). crt0
(`_start`) enables the L1 I/D caches in its first 3 instructions
(`csrsi mcache_ctl,1; csrw mcache_ctl,0x703`). A hybrid window whose handoff
point is AFTER crt0 (`--trigger pc --pc-start <main>`, or `--trigger marker`)
ran QEMU through crt0 (QEMU has no cache model), then vsim resumed with
`mcache_ctl` at reset = caches OFF -> whole measured region ran uncached -> ~4x
inflated window_cycles vs the cycle model.

**Symptom to recognize:** a hybrid window reports MORE cycles than the
whole-program cycle model, or a smaller sub-window costs more than a superset
that starts at `_start`. That superset-cheaper-than-subset is impossible unless
cache-enable state differs -> suspect a dropped machine-setup CSR.

**The fix (4 edit sites, the standard transport pattern):**
- `include/hybrid/state_abi.h`: added `uint64_t mcache_ctl; uint64_t mmisc_ctl;`
  after `fcsr`, shrank `reserved[208]->[192]` (size unchanged, no version bump);
  updated `state_abi_check.h` offset asserts.
- `qemu_plugin/hybrid_handoff.c`: VcpuRegs handles + `find_reg("mcache_ctl"/"mmisc_ctl")`
  + `s.mcache_ctl/mmisc_ctl = read_reg64(...)` in drain_state_into.
- `verilator/src/hybrid/resume_driver.hpp`: `kCsrMcacheCtl=0x7CA`, `kCsrMmiscCtl=0x7D0`;
  `write_csr_tolerant(...)` for both, placed BEFORE the mcycle restore.
- Tests: new resume unit case + ABI layout asserts (host doctest), all 43 e2e pass.

**Why QEMU transport works:** QEMU's Andes fork stores these (write_mcache_ctl
masks+stores into env->andes_csr), `andes_csr_init` merges andes_csr_ops into the
global csr_ops, and the gdbstub csr feature emits them by name (predicate
isz_dsz passes when caches are configured). The plugin reads them by name.

**Verified:** hybrid pc `[main 0x100074, _exit 0x100474]` on hello.elf dropped
14707 -> 2871 cycles (now < whole-program 3632, the correct subset relationship).

**Still open (rest of L21):** other Andes vendor CSRs (mmsc_cfg, micm_cfg,
mdcm_cfg, mxstatus, ...) are still not transported; only the cache/misc-ctl pair
is. Docs: CLAUDE.md "CSR restore split" updated; limitations notebook L21 ->
PARTIAL (quick-ref + Tier-3 cell + demo notebook re-run still pending). Related:
[[project_vsim_halt_slack]].

skills.content:
`/simplify → 4 cleanup agents in parallel → apply the fixes`

You are improving the quality of the changed code, not hunting for bugs. Review
it for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude issues, then fix what you
find. Do not look for correctness bugs — that is what `/code-review` is for.

## Phase 0 — Gather the diff

Run `git diff @{upstream}...HEAD` (or `git diff main...HEAD` / `git diff HEAD~1`
if there's no upstream) to get the unified diff under review. If there are
uncommitted changes, or the range diff is empty, also run `git diff HEAD` and
include the working-tree changes in scope — the review often runs before the
commit. If a PR number, branch name, or file path was passed as an argument,
review that target instead. Treat this diff as the review scope.

## Phase 1 — Review (4 cleanup agents in parallel)

Launch **4 independent review agents** via the Agent tool, all in a
single message so they run concurrently. Pass each agent the diff and one of
the four angles below. Each returns its findings with `file`, `line`, a
one-line `summary`, and the concrete cost (what is duplicated, wasted, or
harder to maintain).

### Reuse

Flag new code that re-implements something the codebase
already has — Grep shared/utility modules and files adjacent to the change,
and name the existing helper to call instead.

### Simplification

Flag unnecessary complexity the diff adds: redundant or derivable state,
copy-paste with slight variation, deep nesting, dead code left behind. Name
the simpler form that does the same job.

### Efficiency

Flag wasted work the diff introduces: redundant computation or repeated I/O,
independent operations run sequentially, blocking work added to startup or
hot paths. Also flag long-lived objects built from closures or captured
environments — they keep the entire enclosing scope alive for the object's
lifetime (a memory leak when that scope holds large values); prefer a
class/struct that copies only the fields it needs. Name the cheaper
alternative.

### Altitude

Check that each change is implemented at the right depth, not as a fragile
bandaid. Special cases layered on shared infrastructure are a sign the fix
isn't deep enough — prefer generalizing the underlying mechanism over adding
special cases.

## Phase 2 — Apply the fixes

Wait for all four agents to complete, dedup findings that point at the same
line or mechanism, and fix each remaining one directly. Skip any finding whose
fix would change intended behavior, require changes well outside the reviewed
diff, or that you judge to be a false positive — note the skip rather than
arguing with it. Finish with a brief summary of what was fixed and what was
skipped (or confirm the code was already clean).

<cell id="cell-0"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type># andes-sim tutorial: guest memory (`--mem-size`)

Every model defaults to a small guest memory (128 MiB). This tutorial
shows how to request more with one flag, what each model does with it,
and where the bytes actually live.

You will:

1. build a program that needs 2 GiB of guest memory,
2. watch it fault under the default, then fix it with `--mem-size`,
3. learn the 2 GiB cap (the AE350 DRAM window) and how each model
   reports it,
4. see the hybrid model's backing-store tiers (`/dev/shm`, then
   `~/.cache/andes-sim`) and how to pin one,
5. check your machine with `andes-sim doctor`.</cell id="cell-0">
<cell id="cell-1">import os
from pathlib import Path
root = next(str(d) for d in (Path.cwd(), *Path.cwd().parents)
            if (d / "build" / "andes-sim").exists())
os.chdir(root)
os.environ["PATH"] = f"{root}/build:" + os.environ["PATH"]
print("working dir:", root)</cell id="cell-1">

working dir: /home/nick/work/hybrid_sim

<cell id="cell-2"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type>## 1. A program that needs 2 GiB

The program writes a pattern at `0x7FFFF000` - 4 KiB below the top of
the 2 GiB DRAM window - and verifies it twice: once immediately, and
once inside the ROI markers (on a hybrid run that second check executes
on the RTL engine, after the handoff).

It links against the vplat runtime, so the same binary runs on every
model, and a `printf` inside the ROI is allowed (it bottoms out in a
UART both engines model):</cell id="cell-2">
<cell id="cell-3">%%bash
. ./config.env 2>/dev/null      # sets HYBRID_TOOLCHAIN
GCC="$HYBRID_TOOLCHAIN/bin/riscv64-unknown-elf-gcc"

cat > highmem.c <<'EOF'
/* A program that needs 2 GiB of guest memory: it stores a pattern
 * 4 KiB below the top of the AE350 DRAM window (0x0 .. 0x80000000)
 * and checks it twice -- once right away, once inside the ROI. */
#include <stdint.h>
#include <stdio.h>
#include <andes_sim/ROI.h>

#define HI ((volatile uint64_t *)0x7FFFF000ull)   /* 2 GiB - 4 KiB */

int main(void)
{
  HI[0] = 0x1122334455667788ull;
  HI[1] = 0xCAFEF00DDEADBEEFull;

  uint64_t a = HI[0], b = HI[1];
  if (a != 0x1122334455667788ull || b != 0xCAFEF00DDEADBEEFull) {
    printf("FAIL: nothing at 0x7FFFF000 -- not enough guest memory\n");
    return 1;
  }
  printf("store+readback at 0x7FFFF000 (2 GiB - 4 KiB): OK\n");

  andes_sim_ROI_begin();
  a = HI[0]; b = HI[1];           /* on hybrid this read runs on the RTL */
  if (a == 0x1122334455667788ull && b == 0xCAFEF00DDEADBEEFull)
    printf("PASS: the ROI sees the pattern at 2 GiB - 4 KiB\n");
  else
    printf("FAIL: pattern lost\n");
  andes_sim_ROI_end();
  return 0;
}
EOF

"$GCC" -march=rv64gc -mabi=lp64d -O1 \
  -I build/runtime/include \
  -B build/runtime -specs=andes-sim.specs highmem.c -o highmem.elf

echo "built:"; file highmem.elf</cell id="cell-3">

built:
highmem.elf: ELF 64-bit LSB executable, UCB RISC-V, RVC, double-float ABI, version 1 (SYSV), statically linked, not stripped

<cell id="cell-4"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type>## 2. The default is small - watch it fault

`--model fast` is QEMU as-is: andes-sim does not inject any memory
setting, so QEMU's own 128 MiB default applies. A load at 2 GiB has no
memory behind it, and the runtime's trap handler reports a load access
fault (`Exception code: 5`) at exactly our address (`mtval:
0x7ffff000`):</cell id="cell-4">
<cell id="cell-5">!andes-sim run --model fast highmem.elf</cell id="cell-5">

[31m[ERROR] Trap occurred![0m
[31m[ERROR] mcause: 0x5[0m
[31m[ERROR] mdcause: 0x62[0m
[31m[ERROR] mepc: 0x100094[0m
[31m[ERROR] mtval: 0x7ffff000[0m
[31m[ERROR] Exception code: 5[0m

<cell id="cell-6"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type>Request the memory and the same binary passes. On `fast` the flag
just forwards a plain `-m 2048M` to QEMU - nothing else changes (and a
`-m` you pass yourself after `--` would still win):</cell id="cell-6">
<cell id="cell-7">!andes-sim run --model fast --mem-size 2G highmem.elf</cell id="cell-7">

store+readback at 0x7FFFF000 (2 GiB - 4 KiB): OK
PASS: the ROI sees the pattern at 2 GiB - 4 KiB

<cell id="cell-8"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type>## 3. The cap: 2 GiB

The AE350 SoC decodes DRAM at `0x0 .. 0x80000000`, so 2 GiB is a hard
ceiling for any QEMU-backed model. Each model reports an over-ask in
its own way - `fast` lets QEMU say it:</cell id="cell-8">
<cell id="cell-9">!andes-sim run --model fast --mem-size 4G highmem.elf</cell id="cell-9">

qemu-system-riscv64: Cannot model more than 2GB RAM

<cell id="cell-10"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type>...while `hybrid` rejects it in the driver, **before** allocating
the (potentially huge) backing file - note there is no `[hsim mmap]`
line:</cell id="cell-10">
<cell id="cell-11">!andes-sim run --model hybrid --trigger marker --engine vsim:ax45mpv_premium --mem-size 4G highmem.elf</cell id="cell-11">

andes-sim run --model hybrid: --mem-size 4G exceeds the AE350 DRAM window (2G max)

<cell id="cell-12"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type>(`--model cycle` has nothing to size - the RTL engine always
models its full DRAM window - so there `--mem-size` is validated and
declared a no-op on stderr.)

## 4. hybrid: one flag, three views of the same bytes

On a hybrid run `--mem-size` sizes one shared thing: a sparse file that
is at once

# andes-sim tutorial: guest memory (`--mem-size`)

Every model defaults to a small guest memory (128 MiB). This tutorial
shows how to request more with one flag, what each model does with it,
and where the bytes actually live.

You will:

1. build a program that needs 2 GiB of guest memory,
2. watch it fault under the default, then fix it with `--mem-size`,
3. learn the 2 GiB cap (the AE350 DRAM window) and how each model
   reports it,
4. see the hybrid model's backing-store tiers (`/dev/shm`, then
   `~/.cache/andes-sim`) and how to pin one,
5. check your machine with `andes-sim doctor`.

            if (d / "build" / "andes-sim").exists())
os.chdir(root)
os.environ["PATH"] = f"{root}/build:" + os.environ["PATH"]
print("working dir:", root)

1	# V-scratch reservation: move the transport page out of the program's RAM
2	
3	## Problem (L26)
4	
5	The V-register transport stages 32 vector registers through a 4 KB guest-RAM
6	window at the **compile-time constant** `kVScratchGpa = 0x00FF0000` (15 MB).
7	That address sits *inside* the program's usable RAM, so a program that places
8	data there (large heap, custom linker script, direct addressing) is silently
9	corrupted on every resume -- even if it never uses V. Demonstrated by
10	`tests/fixtures/break_vscratch.S`.
11	
12	## Core architecture (the fix: scheme D)
13	
14	Put the scratch page **just above the program's declared RAM**, by making the
15	physical mmap one page larger than `--mem-size`. The program is told it has
16	`mem_size`; the simulator quietly maps `mem_size + 4 KB` and parks the scratch
17	in the extra page. No program layout can reach a page above its own ceiling
18	without a bug, so the collision class is removed at the root rather than
19	detected after the fact.
20	
21	```
22	            +----------------+ ram_base + mmap_size            (physical top)
23	V scratch ->|  V scratch 4KB |   mmap_size = mem_size + 4 KB
24	            +----------------+ ram_base + mem_size             (program ceiling)
25	            |  program RAM   |   text / data / heap / stack -- all strictly below
26	            +----------------+ ram_base
27	```
28	
29	Scratch GPA = `ram_base + mmap_size - kVScratchBytes` = the **top page of the
30	mmap**. Both legs already receive `mmap_size`, so the address stays a derived
31	value with **no new field to keep in sync** -- the only change vs the naive
32	"top of RAM" is that the mmap is one page bigger than the program's RAM, which
33	lifts the scratch above everything the program can legally address.
34	
35	Invariant that must hold at every step: **the host stager and the vsim
36	Program-Buffer sweep must use the SAME scratch address.** That is why the
37	"runtime GPA" work (F1) lands as one atomic unit across all three users.
38	
39	## Features
40	
41	### F1. Runtime scratch GPA = top page of the mmap span  [state: DONE]
42	- Verified 2026-06-15: host unit suites green -- v_regfile_xfer 3/3,
43	  resume_driver 33/33, state_drain 32/32 (incl. new unset-guard tests), +18
44	  other hybrid suites. vsim builds all 5 CPUs. Full marker e2e 22/22 (incl. V
45	  fixtures + S/U ax66). `break_vscratch.elf` (the L26 repro) now PASSES under
46	  `--model hybrid --engine vsim:ax45mpv_premium` (was a hang) -- the 0x00FF0000
47	  sentinel survives because the V transport relocated to the mmap top page.
48	- Design note: `scratch_gpa` is a required-when-V ctor arg on ResumeDriver /
49	  StateDrain, defaulting to a `kVScratchGpaUnset` sentinel; a V handoff that
50	  reaches the sweep unset throws (no silent transport via a bogus address).
51	  The 60+ non-V unit-test ctor sites pass a stand-in (kScratch); the real glue
52	  (simulator.hpp `v_scratch_gpa()`) threads the live value through the two
53	  controllers.
54	- NOT yet run as e2e: cosim / lockstep V paths (their drain_full /
55	  drain_checkpoint scratch logic is covered at unit level; same threading).
56	- Replace the fixed `kVScratchGpa` constant with `v_scratch_gpa(ram_base,
57	  ram_size) = ram_base + ram_size - kVScratchBytes`. The scratch is the top
58	  `kVScratchBytes` of whatever RAM span is mapped.
59	- Host stager (`stage_v_to_scratch` / `read_v_from_scratch`) computes the
60	  offset as `ram_size - kVScratchBytes` (it already receives the span + base).
61	- `ResumeDriver` / `StateDrain` take the scratch GPA as a required ctor arg
62	  (no silent default) and pass it to `pb_v_data_sweep`.
63	- `simulator.hpp` construction sites compute the GPA from
64	  `platform.main_memory` and pass it down.
65	- After F1 alone the scratch is the top page of `mem_size` (scheme A: inside
66	  program RAM, but far above this runtime's 7 MB stack -- already better than
67	  the mid-RAM 15 MB constant). F2 lifts it above program RAM (scheme D).
68	- Key files: `verilator/src/hybrid/v_regfile_xfer.hpp`, `resume_driver.hpp`,
69	  `state_drain.hpp`, `program_buffer.hpp` (caller), `simulator.hpp`,
70	  `resume_from_qemu.hpp`, `handoff_controller.hpp`, `lockstep_controller.hpp`;
71	  tests `tests/hybrid/v_regfile_xfer.test.cpp`, `resume_driver.test.cpp`,
72	  `state_drain.test.cpp`.
73	- Deps: none.
74	
75	### F2. Map one page above --mem-size; scratch sits above program RAM  [state: DONE]

77	  (= 32*HYBRID_VLEN_BYTES_MAX); v_regfile_xfer's `kVScratchBytes` references it.
78	  Driver helpers `physical_mmap_bytes()` / `max_program_mem_bytes()` (shm.cpp,
79	  unit-tested in infra-test); `run_plan.cpp` allocates + reports the physical
80	  size (program + page); `cmd_run.cpp` caps --mem-size at 2G - page;
81	  `tests/e2e.sh` mmap split into PROGRAM_SIZE + V_SCRATCH_BYTES.

84	  sentinel at the program's LAST page (0x07FFF000 @128M) and PASSES under
85	  hybrid -- the sentinel survives the V transport, proving the scratch moved to

92	- 2 GiB edge: `mem_size + 4 KB` would cross into MROM at 0x80000000, so cap
93	  usable `--mem-size` at `2G - 4 KB` (doc note; 2G was always approximate, L7).

97	  `driver/engine_registry.cpp`, `tests/e2e.sh`; driver unit tests.
98	- Deps: F1.
99	
100	### F3. Load-time overlap check (loud abort)  [state: DONE]
101	- Verified 2026-06-16: `elf_load_top()` (elf_syms.cpp) returns the highest
102	  PT_LOAD `p_paddr + p_memsz`; `cmd_run.cpp` rejects a hybrid run when that

108	- Scope: static image only (PT_LOAD). Runtime heap/stack growth into the

113	  ceiling" case from silent corruption into a clear error.
114	- Key files: driver ELF loader / vsim `state_loader.hpp`; new unit test.
115	- Deps: F1, F2.
116

detected after the fact.

```
            +----------------+ ram_base + mmap_size            (physical top)
V scratch ->|  V scratch 4KB |   mmap_size = mem_size + 4 KB
            +----------------+ ram_base + mem_size             (program ceiling)
            |  program RAM   |   text / data / heap / stack -- all strictly below
            +----------------+ ram_base
```

Scratch GPA = `ram_base + mmap_size - kVScratchBytes` = the **top page of the
mmap**. Both legs already receive `mmap_size`, so the address stays a derived
value with **no new field to keep in sync** -- the only change vs the naive
"top of RAM" is that the mmap is one page bigger than the program's RAM, which
lifts the scratch above everything the program can legally address.

Invariant that must hold at every step: **the host stager and the vsim
Program-Buffer sweep must use the SAME scratch address.** That is why the
"runtime GPA" work (F1) lands as one atomic unit across all three users.

### F1. Runtime scratch GPA = top page of the mmap span  [state: DONE]
- Verified 2026-06-15: host unit suites green -- v_regfile_xfer 3/3,
  resume_driver 33/33, state_drain 32/32 (incl. new unset-guard tests), +18
  other hybrid suites. vsim builds all 5 CPUs. Full marker e2e 22/22 (incl. V
  fixtures + S/U ax66). `break_vscratch.elf` (the L26 repro) now PASSES under
  `--model hybrid --engine vsim:ax45mpv_premium` (was a hang) -- the 0x00FF0000
  sentinel survives because the V transport relocated to the mmap top page.
- Design note: `scratch_gpa` is a required-when-V ctor arg on ResumeDriver /
  StateDrain, defaulting to a `kVScratchGpaUnset` sentinel; a V handoff that
  reaches the sweep unset throws (no silent transport via a bogus address).
  The 60+ non-V unit-test ctor sites pass a stand-in (kScratch); the real glue
  (simulator.hpp `v_scratch_gpa()`) threads the live value through the two
  controllers.
- NOT yet run as e2e: cosim / lockstep V paths (their drain_full /
  drain_checkpoint scratch logic is covered at unit level; same threading).
- Replace the fixed `kVScratchGpa` constant with `v_scratch_gpa(ram_base,
  ram_size) = ram_base + ram_size - kVScratchBytes`. The scratch is the top
  `kVScratchBytes` of whatever RAM span is mapped.
- Host stager (`stage_v_to_scratch` / `read_v_from_scratch`) computes the
  offset as `ram_size - kVScratchBytes` (it already receives the span + base).

  (no silent default) and pass it to `pb_v_data_sweep`.

  `platform.main_memory` and pass it down.

  program RAM, but far above this runtime's 7 MB stack -- already better than
  the mid-RAM 15 MB constant). F2 lifts it above program RAM (scheme D).
- Key files: `verilator/src/hybrid/v_regfile_xfer.hpp`, `resume_driver.hpp`,

  `tests/e2e.sh` mmap split into PROGRAM_SIZE + V_SCRATCH_BYTES.

  sentinel at the program's LAST page (0x07FFF000 @128M) and PASSES under

Ground truth confirmed, and it's serious:

- **hybrid `--mem-size 2G`**: rejected (cap is 2G-4KiB). Committed cell 13's success is impossible now.
- **hybrid at the cap (2G-4KiB)**: QEMU readback OK, but vsim reports **"FAIL: pattern lost"** — the program's target `0x7FFFF000` is exactly the reserved scratch page, so the data does not survive into the cycle engine.
- **hybrid below the address**: load fault (exit 5).

So the program's chosen address (2GiB-4KiB) collides head-on with the V-scratch page. The whole section-4 centerpiece is broken by the very reservation I'm documenting. Let me run one control to confirm the mechanism is the top-page scratch (store one page lower, same memory size) before I decide the narrative.
